column6: The commentary stresses that Joseph is imprisoned after his innocence becomes clear; Joseph tells the cupbearer he was taken from his land and has done nothing deserving the dungeon, making the imposed wait an injustice in his own account.
The commentary follows the dreamer whose pressed grapes precede release; Joseph gives the other prisoner a three-day prediction of execution, so the shared prison interval leads to opposite ends.

column5: Joseph brought out of the pit
column6: The commentary's delayed prison years finally end in rescue; Pharaoh summons Joseph and he is hurried out of the dungeon, marking the actual release after the forgotten request.

The commentary makes the sheltered harvest available after the hard years begin and hears asr as gain; people from all lands come to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph because famine spreads, making storage a wider rescue and transaction.

The commentary lays Joseph's release and stored crop across a measured calendar; Joseph tells his brothers that two famine years have passed and five remain without plowing or harvest, specifying the continuing span that stored grain must cover.

column5: wages placed in a bag with holes
column6: The commentary's time is capital and pressing separates valuable flow from residue; Haggai says people sow much but harvest little and earn wages only to put them in a pierced bag, an exact image of labor's yield leaking away.

The commentary reads the ruined garden as a picture of moral loss after withheld good; Isaiah identifies the vineyard as Israel and says God expected justice but found bloodshed, giving the garden's failed crop its ethical referent.

column5: blessing remains inside a grape cluster
column6: The commentary separates extracted good from dry remainder and makes rescue an exception to loss; Isaiah says not to destroy a cluster because new wine is found in it and uses that reason to spare some servants.

The commentary's generous hand, guarded harvest, and endangered garden meet here; after the tithe promise, God says he will rebuke the devourer so crops are not destroyed and the vine does not fail to bear.

The commentary makes rain or its restraint determine whether stored effort yields food; God says he withheld rain three months before harvest and sent it on one city but not another, joining timed scarcity and uneven release.
The commentary's pressed cloud behaves like a container whose water is released; God's question about who can tip the water jars of the heavens supplies another concrete vessel image for rainfall.

The commentary contrasts released water with compressed dry residue; Job's next question describes dust hardening into a mass and clods sticking together, the arid earth after the heavenly jars image.

The commentary traces squeezed cloud to grain, plant, and provision; Isaiah says rain and snow water earth, make it sprout, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, a full agricultural sequence.

The commentary contrasts withholding with a pressured hand that gives; Elijah tells the widow with a final meal in view to first make him a small cake, making her scarce provision the test of release.

column5: flour and oil survive the drought
column6: The commentary's protected contents last through lean time after a gift; the widow's flour jar does not empty and her oil jug does not run dry, just as Elijah had promised.

The commentary joins enclosure to a beneficial outflow rather than mere retention; Elisha tells the widow to close the door behind her and her sons and pour her small supply of oil into gathered vessels.

column5: sell oil, pay debt, live on remainder
column6: The commentary hears squeezing and stored yield as income that can rescue a household; Elisha tells the widow to sell the multiplied oil, discharge her debt, and live with her sons on what remains.

column5: winepress yield given to freed servant
column6: The commentary's press product becomes a gift when the hand releases it; Deuteronomy commands an owner freeing a servant to provide generously from flock, threshing floor, and winepress.

column5: cloak returned by sunset as shelter
column6: The commentary pairs the day's closing edge with whether one holds back another's protection; the creditor must return a poor person's pledged cloak by sunset so that person can sleep in it.

column5: heaven and earth hear before verdict
column6: The commentary's opening oath suspends its judgment until the next line; Moses first summons heaven and earth to hear his speech before his song states God's ways and Israel's response, another cosmic opening that makes the following verdict weighty.

column5: persecuted people seek wilderness hiding places
column6: The commentary's youths withdraw from hostile worship to a hidden refuge; royal officers learn that Jewish families who rejected the king's command have fled to wilderness hiding places, giving flight and shelter a similar social cause.

The commentary's hidden refuge protects faithful youths across a long interval; the fugitives in 1 Maccabees die with their families when attacked on the Sabbath, a pointed reversal of safety after flight.

column5: open to receive, shut to repay
column6: The commentary's grasp can receive while refusing to release; Sirach warns against stretching the hand out to take and closing it when repayment is due, exactly distinguishing the two directions of a hand.

column5: alms stored for a day of need
column6: The commentary's productive gift and future shelter meet when Tobit says almsgiving stores a good treasure against a day of necessity, making generosity a reserve rather than depletion.

column5: hands open to receive, closed to give
column6: The commentary's asr images make grasping ethically double; the Didache forbids extending the hands to receive while drawing them back when it is time to give, making the hand's direction the whole contrast.
The commentary names taking back a previous gift as a form of squeezing; the Didache tells hearers to give to those who ask and not demand it back, an exact ethical opposite to reclaimed donation.

The commentary reads a barren or lost garden against the time left to work; the vineyard owner has sought fruit from his fig tree for three years and orders it cut down, measuring unproductive time before loss.

The commentary's late afternoon may still allow a final productive interval; the gardener asks to leave the fig tree one more year while he digs and manures around it, making delay a chance for fruit.
The commentary's pressure yields either benefit or dry loss; the gardener says future fruit will spare the tree, otherwise it can be cut down, completing the time-limited exception.

The commentary's garden owners plan to keep all produce; in Jesus' vineyard parable the owner sends servants to receive his fruit when harvest time arrives, setting up a precise conflict over what must be handed over.
The commentary's withheld crop brings the holders' loss; the hearers say the owner will destroy the violent tenants and lease the vineyard to others who will deliver fruit in season.

The commentary makes constriction either draw out good fruit or leave a dry loss; Jesus says the vinedresser removes branches without fruit and prunes fruiting ones for more yield, distinguishing two outcomes of cutting.
The commentary's garden is ruined while its keepers sleep and appears lost at daybreak; the disciples see Jesus' fig tree withered to its roots as they pass it in the morning.

column5: farmer waits for early and late rain
column6: The commentary's crop survives a long interval before the year of pressing; James tells readers to be patient like a farmer waiting for precious fruit and early and late rains, tying endurance to delayed yield.

column5: rain makes land useful and blessed
column6: The commentary's pressed cloud starts a chain from water to benefit; Hebrews says land that drinks repeated rain and produces a useful crop receives blessing, then uses that field to describe the hearers' response.
The commentary's destroyed garden is the loss side of a moral agricultural image; Hebrews contrasts land bearing thorns, near a curse and ending in fire, with the rain-fed useful crop just described.
The commentary's late-coming hour can turn protected waiting into missed opportunity; in the bridesmaids' parable the bridegroom is delayed and all fall asleep, setting up the later closed door.
The commentary's shelter can preserve those inside through a span while others lose entry; prepared bridesmaids enter the wedding and the door is shut when the bridegroom comes.

column5: unknown day and hour require watchfulness
column6: The commentary's unnamed asr leaves its exact temporal extent open while the coming judgment matters; Jesus concludes the bridesmaids' scene by telling hearers to watch because they do not know the day or hour.

The commentary's cave shelters believers from hostility across centuries; Revelation shows rulers and others hiding in caves and rocks when judgment arrives, making a cave a place of fear rather than assured rescue.

column5: cave dwellers ask rocks to hide them
column6: The commentary's protected sleepers can leave their cave in mercy; Revelation's terrified people instead ask mountains and rocks to conceal them from the enthroned one, so earthly enclosure cannot promise safety.
The commentary's believers leave their people and find refuge in a cave; Hebrews recalls faithful sufferers wandering deserts, mountains, caves, and holes of earth because of persecution.
The commentary contrasts a hand that retains wealth with one that lets benefit flow; the wealthy are instructed to do good, be rich in works, and be generous and ready to share.
The commentary lets a gift function as lasting provision after ordinary stores fail; the next verse calls sharing a good foundation stored for the future so the givers may take hold of real life.
The commentary's accumulated yield can disappear at the wrong hour; Jesus warns against storing treasure on earth, where moth, corrosion, and thieves destroy or take it.
The commentary's guarded grain and refuge suggest a store that endures; Jesus tells hearers to store treasure in heaven where the stated destroyers and thieves cannot reach it.

column5: spend wealth to gain lasting welcome
column6: The commentary asks whether today's capital yields generosity and shelter later; Jesus says to make friends through worldly wealth so that when it fails they may welcome the giver into enduring dwellings.
The commentary lets the day and a whole life contract toward their end; Paul says the remaining time has been shortened and immediately revises how ordinary attachments are to be held.
The commentary's oath gives force to a later verdict about human loss; the angel proclaims that the hour of God's judgment has come and calls people to fear and worship him.

column5: heavens withhold dew after failed harvest
column6: The commentary's cloud release or closure governs agricultural gain; Haggai says the heavens withheld dew and the earth withheld its produce, supplying the weather side of the pierced-wages lament.
The commentary joins raised storm cloud, rain, and vegetation; Zechariah urges asking the LORD for spring rain and says he makes storm clouds and showers that give plants to every field.
The commentary's stored grain and patience can turn present hardship into eventual yield; the psalm says those sowing in tears will reap with joy, joining time, grain, and reversed loss.

column5: fugitive prophet shelters in a cave
column6: The commentary's youths flee their community into a cave; Elijah reaches a cave and lodges there before hearing the LORD's question, a briefer prophetic refuge without a centuries-long sleep.

column5: caves from fear of divine rising
column6: The commentary's cave opens room for mercy to endangered believers; Isaiah's people enter rock caves and ground holes from the LORD's terror, giving enclosure a contrary meaning at judgment.
The commentary makes the difference between grasping and giving depend on what leaves the hand; Tobit instructs his son to give alms from his property and not turn his face away from the poor.

The commentary's shrinking time remains a place to prepare for what follows; Avot compares this world to a vestibule before the world to come and tells the hearer to prepare there before entering the hall.

The commentary holds a lifetime and a brief final interval together; Avot says one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world exceeds the whole life of the coming world in that respect, placing moral weight on a small unit of time.

The commentary's same grasp can make a giver or a miser; Avot's four property dispositions include treating one's own as another's and another's as another's for the generous case, versus taking both for oneself in the wicked case.

column5: master shuts door to late arrivals
column6: The commentary's time-bound refuge suggests a threshold that can close; Jesus describes a householder shutting the door while people stand outside and ask to be admitted too late.

The commentary's late-day work depends on a finite span of light; Jesus asks whether there are twelve hours in the day and says walking in daylight keeps one from stumbling, elaborating the same time-to-act image as his later saying.

The commentary's delayed relief in Joseph's story and the sleeper's long interval can be heard as purposive waiting; 2 Peter says the Lord is not slow about the promise but patient, giving a specific interpretive bridge for delay.
